result: The authors demonstrate that dextran molecules of different sizes differentially penetrate matrigel based on their gyration radius. Small dextran (<5 nm, <70 kDa) permeates the ECM meshwork and compresses cells, while big dextran (>15 nm, >500 kDa) is excluded from the ECM and compresses the entire aggregate by dehydrating the ECM.
evaluation: Claims C6-C9 are well-supported by fluorescence imaging data (Figure 2a) showing differential penetration of dextran molecules into matrigel beads based on size, with appropriate citation to Granath, 1958 for molecular weight-size relationships. The visual evidence clearly demonstrates the size-dependent exclusion principle.

result: The authors show that matrigel beads compress by 63±5% under 5 kPa pressure from big dextran, while multicellular spheroids have an effective osmotic modulus of ~30 kPa (15-fold smaller than individual cells) and show no measurable volume change with small dextran at moderate pressures (up to 10 kPa).
evaluation: Claims C11, C13, and C14 are supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2b-d with appropriate error bars and statistical analysis. The differential compressibility between matrigel, individual cells, and MCS is clearly demonstrated with proper controls and replication.

result: Theoretical modeling predicts that both small and big dextran lead to the same cell volume loss, which depends only on the cell volume regulation system and not on ECM mechanical properties.
evaluation: Claim C15 is supported by theoretical derivations in Appendix A.5, with the model providing Equation 1 that shows cell volume change depends on osmotic pressure and ion pumping parameters but not ECM mechanics. The theoretical framework is internally consistent with the experimental observations.

result: Small dextran at 40 kPa induces a ~35±10% increase in interstitial fluorescence (indicating ECM swelling), while big dextran causes a 50% loss of interstitial fluorescence (indicating ECM dehydration and compression).
evaluation: Claims C20-C21 are supported by two-photon fluorescence microscopy measurements (Figure 3c) with appropriate normalization procedures and quantification methods described in Materials and Methods. The opposite effects of small vs. big dextran on interstitial space are clearly demonstrated.

result: Global compression with big dextran stops cell division in the MCS core and alters overall growth, with Ki67-positive cell density uniformly decreasing under pressure. The periphery-to-core ratio of proliferating cells increases from 2 (no pressure) to 2.5 (small dextran) to 5 (big dextran).
evaluation: Claims C22-C25 are supported by Ki67 immunostaining data (Figure 4a-b) with spatial analysis across the spheroid radius. The quantification shows clear differences between conditions with appropriate sample sizes (9-26 MCS per condition) and statistical analysis, consistent with prior literature.

result: MCS growth rate (doubling time) almost doubled under big dextran compression, increasing from 36±1 hr (control and small dextran) to 68±4 hr (big dextran).
evaluation: Claim C26 is supported by longitudinal volumetric measurements (Figure 4c-d) tracking spheroid growth over multiple days with clear exponential fitting and appropriate error quantification. The differential effect of big vs. small dextran on growth rate is statistically significant.

result: Cell migration speed within MCS was reduced by 50% at 5 kPa with big dextran compared to unstressed conditions, while both proliferation and motility remained almost unaltered with small dextran at the same pressure.
evaluation: Claims C27-C28 are supported by Dynamic Light Scattering measurements (Figure 4e) with N=5 independent experiments and appropriate statistical analysis. The selective effect of ECM compression (big dextran) vs. cell compression alone (small dextran) is clearly demonstrated.

result: Individual cells plated on Petri dishes show no change in proliferation or motility when exposed to 5 kPa dextran pressure, with division times remaining ~11 hr regardless of dextran size or presence.
evaluation: Claims C29, C80-C82 are supported by measurements on 2D cultured cells (Figure 4f-g) demonstrating that dextran at 5 kPa has no direct effect on isolated cells in the absence of ECM. This control experiment is critical for establishing that ECM is required for the mechanosensitive response.

result: Cells embedded in matrigel show different phenotypes depending on compression state: cells in relaxed or small dextran-treated MG are sparse with numerous protrusions and high anisotropy, while cells in compressed MG (big dextran) proliferate locally, appear smooth, and form round mini-spheroids.
evaluation: Claims C30-C34 are supported by imaging data (Figure 5a-b) showing clear morphological differences in cell shape and distribution. Actin labeling provides direct evidence of cytoskeletal organization changes. The inference that MG compression inhibits motility and promotes mini-spheroid formation is reasonable given the visual evidence.

result: Cells embedded in compressed matrigel are nearly immobile, while cells in relaxed matrigel migrate with velocities comparable to those on flat surfaces.
evaluation: Claims C35-C36 are supported by cell tracking data (Figure 5c-d) showing ~40 trajectories per condition with clear quantification of migration speeds. The dramatic difference in motility between compressed and relaxed MG conditions is visually and quantitatively evident.

result: Cell proliferation rate drops considerably when matrigel is compressed with big dextran compared to no pressure or small dextran conditions. Matrigel density (2-8 g/l) has little to no effect on cell proliferation.
evaluation: Claims C40-C41 are supported by Hoechst fluorescence measurements over time (Figure 5e, 5g) with N=15 samples from 8 independent experiments. The control experiment varying MG concentration (Figure 5g) effectively rules out that increased matrix density per se is responsible for reduced proliferation.

result: The main conclusion is that compressive stress transmitted to cells by the surrounding ECM, rather than direct osmotic pressure on cells, strongly impacts cell motility and proliferation. Global compressions affect aggregate growth and motility, while selective cell compressions of the same magnitude have minimal effect. The ECM acts as a mechanical sensor regulating cell behavior in 3D environments.
evaluation: Claims C42, C63-C66 represent the central thesis supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence from all prior results. The selective compression method successfully decouples cell volume changes from ECM mechanical stress, and the differential biological responses (proliferation, motility, morphology) clearly demonstrate ECM's mechanosensory role. The conclusion is well-justified by converging evidence from multiple experimental systems.

result: Fibronectin is abundant in the interstitial space of CT26 MCS, the ECM is 100-1000-fold more compressible than cells, drugs affecting cytoskeleton have negligible effects on MCS compressibility, and volume loss under compression is mainly due to ECM dehydration.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C4, C5 establish the foundational properties of the MCS system. C1 is supported by immunofluorescence (Figure 1a, Appendix 8), C2 is stated as known property, C4 is supported by data in Appendix 12, and C5 is supported by citation to Dolega et al., 2021. These claims provide necessary context for the main experiments.

result: Osmotic pressure of a few kPa strongly reduces cell proliferation within multicellular aggregates but has no effect on individual cells cultured on Petri dishes in the absence of ECM.
evaluation: Claim C3 is supported by citation to prior work (Montel et al., 2011) and is consistent with the current study's findings (C29). This establishes the key motivation for investigating ECM's role in mechanosensing.

result: Weak osmotic pressures (~1 kPa) have no measurable effect on cell volume due to active regulatory processes, yet both proliferation and motility decrease in MCS under weak compression. For such weak compressions, cell volume is unchanged while the ECM is directly impacted.
evaluation: Claims C45-C48 synthesize key observations from the study with appropriate citations (Hoffmann et al., 2009; Cadart et al., 2019). The claims are consistent with the experimental data showing differential effects of small vs. big dextran and establish the pressure range where ECM mechanics dominate over cell volume effects.

result: Large pressures (~100 kPa) can cause cell volume decrease and nuclear deformation, and cell/nuclear volume can be key to proliferation, invasion, and differentiation.
evaluation: Claims C43-C44 cite relevant prior work (Zhou et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2017; Han et al., 2020) to establish context for why the current study focuses on weak pressures where volume effects are negligible. These are appropriately cited background claims.

result: The mechano-sensitive role of ECM could explain why osmotic and mechanical pressures similarly affect MCS growth. Potential mechanisms include contact inhibition from reduced interstitial space, reduced ECM permeability affecting nutrient/oxygen diffusion, though proliferation inhibition is probably not related to hypoxia/starvation based on single-cell experiments.
evaluation: Claims C49, C51-C54 present speculative mechanisms for how ECM compression affects cell behavior. While C49 and C53 are supported by citations, C51-C52 are explicitly speculative ('may activate'). C54's inference that hypoxia/starvation are not responsible is reasonable but not definitively proven. These represent plausible hypotheses requiring further validation.

result: ECM microscopic structure is modified under compression (density increase, reduced porosity) affecting rheology. Compression increases ECM bulk modulus and causes non-linear stiffness changes. ECM rheological properties affect cell growth through stretch-activated channels, and integrin-dependent signals are regulated by cell-ECM stress/strain.
evaluation: Claims C55-C58 synthesize relevant prior work (Sopher et al., 2018; Kurniawan et al., 2016; Nam et al., 2019; multiple others) to provide mechanistic context for the observed biological responses. These are appropriately cited background claims that frame potential molecular mechanisms.

result: ECM is strongly modified in tumors with solid stress reaching several kPa. In tumors, the collagen/hyaluronan ratio decreases, and hyaluronan (more hydrophilic than collagen) tends to swell and stiffen ECM. The correlation between matrix mechanics and uncontrolled proliferation is increasingly accepted.
evaluation: Claims C59-C62 cite relevant oncology literature (Nia et al., 2017; Voutouri et al., 2016; Bissell et al., 2002; Lelièvre and Bissell, 2006; Broders-Bondon et al., 2018) to establish the pathophysiological relevance of the findings. These appropriately contextualize the work's implications for cancer biology.

result: Background claims establishing that imposed deformations affect morphogenesis and homeostasis, ECM provides scaffolding and triggers mechanotransduction, changing ECM mechanics can reverse aging/accelerate development/modulate tumor malignancy, mechanical context is important in cancer, tumor growth is modulated by self-generated compression, and MCS growth is reduced under confinement or osmotic compression.
evaluation: Claims C67-C79 are introductory/background statements supported by appropriate citations to establish the scientific context and motivation for the study. These are standard literature review claims that accurately represent prior work in the field.
